16805 ms: ● How a Lighthouse Works
16805 ms:   A lighthouse is a tower that marks a dangerous or important point on the coast so that ships can navigate safely,
16805 ms:   especially at night or in poor visibility. Its three main parts are:
16805 ms:                                                                                                                           - The light source. A lamp, once an oil or gas flame and now usually an LED, produces the beam.
16805 ms:   - The optic. A system of lenses and prisms, often a Fresnel lens, gathers the light from the lamp and focuses it into
16805 ms:     a concentrated beam instead of letting it spread in all directions.
16805 ms:   - The rotating mechanism. A clockwork or motor turns the optic so the beam sweeps across the horizon. Each lighthouse
16805 ms:     has its own flash pattern, so sailors can tell which light they are seeing.
16805 ms:   The lamp sits at the center of the optic, and the optic is mounted on a turntable or inside a rotating drum. Its
16805 ms:   curved glass panels bend light that would otherwise escape upward or downward into a narrow horizontal band. The
16805 ms:   result is a beam that is much brighter at sea than the bare flame would be, and the rotation makes it appear as a
16805 ms:   flash rather than a steady glow.
16805 ms:   The tower\'s height matters as well. A higher light can be seen from farther away, because the curve of the Earth
16805 ms:   limits how far a light near the water can reach the horizon. Modern lighthouses often run automatically on solar or
16805 ms:   mains power, and many now use GPS and radio beacons alongside the light, but the basic principle of a focused,
16805 ms:   rotating beam that identifies a location has not changed for about two centuries.
